A confidante is a person you trust so deeply that you feel safe sharing your most private thoughts, secrets, fears, worries, and personal problems with them — knowing with full confidence that they will keep everything to themselves and not judge you.

Think of it this way: Most people in your life know you, but a confidante knows the real, unfiltered you — the version of you that you hide from the rest of the world.

The entire word revolves around one concept: trust of the deepest kind.

When you share something with a confidante, you are not just gossiping or chatting. You are confiding — meaning you are revealing something personal and private because you trust this person completely. A confidante is the person you call at 2 a.m. when something is weighing heavily on your heart. They are the person you tell things to that you would never say out loud to anyone else.

A confidante typically does three things:

  • Listens without interrupting or dismissing you
  • Keeps your secrets without ever sharing them with others
  • Supports you emotionally, without judging you for what you've shared
A Confidante vs. A Regular Friend

This is an important distinction. Not every friend is a confidante, and not every confidante is necessarily a friend in the typical sense.

You might have many friends you enjoy spending time with — laughing, going out, sharing hobbies. But among all those people, only one or two might be your true confidantes. The difference is the level of trust and emotional depth.

With a regular friend → you share good times, opinions, and everyday thoughts.
With a confidante → you share your innermost self — your anxieties, your shame, your deepest desires, your greatest fears.

A confidante is someone you have chosen to let behind the curtain of your public self. That choice is never made lightly.

Traditionally, confidante (spelled with an "e" at the end) was used specifically for a woman who holds this trusted role, while confidant (without the "e") was used for a man. This comes from how European languages used to assign gender to words.

However, in modern everyday English, this distinction has largely faded. You will often see "confidante" used for any person, regardless of gender. Both spellings are widely accepted today in general usage.

In books, plays, and films, a confidante is also a specific type of character — a trusted companion of the main character who exists largely so the main character can speak their private thoughts out loud. Without the confidante character, the audience would have no way of knowing what the hero or heroine is truly feeling inside. The confidante gives the main character someone to talk to, which gives you — the reader or viewer — a window into the story's inner world. Think of a princess talking openly to her loyal lady-in-waiting, or a troubled protagonist pouring their heart out to their best friend.

• "After her divorce, her sister became her closest confidante — the only person she could be completely honest with."
  • "The CEO confided in her assistant, who had been her confidante for over twenty years."
  • "He was not just a mentor; over time, he became a trusted confidante who knew all of the young man's doubts and dreams."
  • "In the novel, the heroine's childhood friend serves as her confidante, hearing every secret thought the heroine cannot say in public."

"Confidante" is a warm, meaningful, and slightly rare word. When you call someone your confidante, you are not just saying they are a good listener — you are saying that they hold a sacred piece of your inner life. The word carries a sense of emotional intimacy, loyalty, and deep personal trust. It describes a relationship that not everyone is lucky enough to have, and which, when found, is truly precious.

A confidante is a deeply trusted person — often a close friend — to whom you privately share your secrets, fears, and true feelings, knowing they will listen without judgment and guard what you've shared with complete loyalty.
